experiment: is the prefill gap my kernel's deficiency or a TileLang-vs-vendor capability limit?
method: benchmark TileLang official examples/ascend/example_rmsnorm.py against torch_npu.npu_rms_norm in one window, msprof device time

official_example_fp32_8192x4096.note: TileLang's OWN official RMSNorm example is only 0.69x of the vendor on fp32

results.official_example_bf16: does not run - T.copy cannot cast bf16->fp32 outside a VF block; the official example is fp32-only

key_insight: vendor bf16 (0.051 ms) is ~3x FASTER than vendor fp32 (0.159 ms) on the same shape: the vendor bf16 path is heavily optimised (bf16-native compute / less traffic)
our bf16 kernel upcasts to fp32 for the statistics (the precision gate demands fp32 accumulation), so it pays fp32-level cost on bf16 data - this is why bf16 lands ~0.39x while fp32 lands ~0.69x
the repo's own official RMSNorm uses the same SimtVF structure and does NOT reach vendor parity even on fp32
conclusion: the prefill gap is a TileLang-vs-vendor-implementation capability gap, not a defect of this particular kernel. TileLang's best available RMSNorm (official example, and this kernel's cw4 variant) does not reach the vendor's bf16 operator. Reaching parity needs a bf16-native, vendor-level kernel (SIMD micro-API with bf16 compute that still meets the fp32-stats precision gate) - a research effort beyond parameter tuning or the official example.

review_correction_2026_11_02.note: This record is exploratory, not an acceptance result. The post-hoc co-tenant classifier change, sparse sampling and canary cannot prove absence of interference; 12 pairs in one process do not meet the planned >=15 pairs and >=3 processes. Do not claim EXCEED, a TileLang capability boundary, exhaustive tuning, or a proven mechanism from these measurements. Preserve original values as historical observations pending independent validation.
